planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter while dormant, in deep, well-drained soil with full sun exposure; Comanche is a Type I (protandrous) pollen shedder and should be paired with a Type II cultivar such as Wichita or Cape Fear for full cross-pollination; give it plenty of room since mature trees develop a wide-spreading canopy.

directions: Comanche is a Texas A&M-era release prized for bearing at a younger age than most older pecan cultivars, often producing a first meaningful crop within six to seven years of planting rather than the decade or more typical of seedling trees. The kernels are medium-large with rich, sweet flavor and a bright golden color that scores well in home taste tests. Because it leafs out and blooms fairly early, Comanche can be more exposed to spring frost and, in humid Gulf Coast summers, to pecan scab, so a fungicide program or planting in an open, breezy site helps keep foliage and shuck disease pressure down. Zinc deficiency is common in pecans generally, so annual foliar zinc applications in spring support strong nut fill and healthy leaf growth.

common_name: Lewis Hazelnut (OSU Eastern Filbert Blight-Resistant Kernel Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Lewis is self-incompatible and needs a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar planted nearby, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated in late winter before leaves emerge; it was one of the earliest Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant releases from the Oregon State University breeding program and largely replaced susceptible older varieties like Barcelona in new Pacific Northwest plantings.

directions: Lewis was released by Oregon State University's hazelnut breeding program as a kernel-quality companion to the more vigorous Clark, combining Eastern Filbert Blight resistance with a round, well-flavored nut suited to fresh eating and roasting. It bears at a relatively young age for a hazelnut, typically producing meaningful crops within three to four years of transplanting, and its moderate size makes it manageable in a home orchard row. Nuts ripen in early fall and drop free of the husk, so growers gather them promptly from the ground to avoid mold and rodent losses. Like other European hazelnuts, Lewis performs best where summers are warm but not excessively humid, and it needs a genetically compatible pollenizer cultivar for reliable nut set.

common_name: Clark Hazelnut (OSU EFB-Resistant Vigorous Commercial Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Clark is self-incompatible and requires a compatible pollenizer cultivar planted within range for wind pollination; it was released by the Oregon State University hazelnut breeding program alongside Lewis as part of the first generation of Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant replacements for Barcelona.

directions: Clark is a vigorous, upright Oregon State University hazelnut release valued by commercial growers for heavy, consistent yields of medium-large, well-filled nuts with good shelf life. Its strong Eastern Filbert Blight resistance, inherited from wild Corylus germplasm bred into the OSU program, has made it one of the varieties that replaced blight-susceptible Barcelona in Willamette Valley orchards. Trees are notably vigorous growers and benefit from an open center or modified vase pruning to keep the canopy productive and allow good spray coverage. Nuts ripen and drop in early autumn and should be collected promptly and dried down before storage to preserve flavor and prevent mold.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sacajawea was bred by Oregon State University primarily as an early-shedding, Eastern Filbert Blight-resistant pollenizer for main-crop cultivars like Jefferson and Yamhill, though it also produces a worthwhile crop of its own nuts.

directions: Sacajawea is an Oregon State University hazelnut release notable for its striking upright, columnar habit and attractive dark reddish-bronze new foliage that ages to green, making it more ornamental in the landscape than most orchard hazelnuts. It was primarily developed as a blight-resistant pollenizer whose pollen shed timing overlaps well with premium kernel cultivars, but it also yields a respectable crop of good-flavored, medium nuts on its own. Its columnar growth habit allows tighter in-row spacing than sprawling older varieties, which is useful in a smaller home orchard. Give it full sun and a companion cultivar for cross-pollination, and harvest promptly from the ground each fall once nuts drop free of the husk.

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil; Payne leafs out and blooms notably early in spring, so it is best sited away from low frost pockets; it is a strong pollen producer and can serve as a pollenizer for other English walnut cultivars in addition to bearing its own crop.

directions: Payne was, for decades, one of California's most widely planted English walnut cultivars, valued for beginning to bear at a young age and for its heavy, precocious cropping compared with older seedling walnuts. Trees stay smaller than many other walnut cultivars, which suits it to home orchards with limited space, and its thin-shelled, light-colored kernels have good flavor for fresh eating and baking. Payne leafs out and blooms early, which increases exposure to spring frost damage and to walnut blight in wet, humid spring weather, so it is generally better suited to drier walnut-growing climates than to the humid Gulf South. Its relatively low chill requirement compared with other English walnuts makes it one of the more mild-winter-tolerant Persian walnut cultivars available.
sources: University of California, Davis Walnut Improvement Program

common_name: Serr Walnut (Historic Large-Nutted UC Davis Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile loam; Serr is a vigorous, precocious cultivar that benefits from cross-pollination with a compatible variety; it was historically a leading commercial cultivar before being largely supplanted by Chandler, but it remains available through specialty nurseries for home orchards.

directions: Serr walnut was released by the University of California, Davis breeding program in 1968 and quickly became a leading commercial cultivar for its precocious bearing, vigorous growth, and very large, well-filled nuts. It gained a reputation for heavy production at a younger age than the older standard varieties of its era, helping accelerate the shift of California walnut orchards toward planned cultivar selection rather than seedling trees. Serr is more susceptible to blackline disease, a graft-incompatibility disorder associated with cherry leafroll virus, than newer releases, which along with the arrival of the higher-quality Chandler cultivar led to its decline in new commercial plantings from the 1980s onward. It remains a historically important cultivar and a useful large-nutted choice for home orchardists in walnut-friendly climates who can source grafted trees.
sources: University of California, Davis Walnut Improvement Program

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost danger has passed; Randy is a male, non-fruiting cultivar selected to shed pollen slightly earlier than Peters, giving growers a way to fine-tune pollen timing against Kerman and other female cultivars whose bloom period varies by site and season.

directions: Randy is a male pistachio cultivar developed as a pollen source alternative to Peters, chosen because its pollen shed window falls slightly earlier, which helps growers extend the overlap with female bloom in orchards where timing between Kerman and Peters does not line up well in a given year. Like all pistachios it needs deep, well-drained, alkaline soil, hundreds of hours of winter chill, and a long, hot, low-humidity summer, so it shares the species' poor fit for humid Gulf Coast gardens even when winter temperatures are mild enough. A single Randy tree, positioned upwind or centrally among female trees, can supply pollen for a number of surrounding fruiting trees since pistachio is entirely wind-pollinated. Because it sets no nut crop itself, Randy can be pruned more aggressively to control its size relative to the female trees it services.
